guides.title: Federation Membership: How a World Joins
guides.summary: How a world joins the United Federation of Planets: the petition, the requirements for membership, the candidacy and evaluation period, and notable admissions and deferrals such as Coridan and Bajor.

sections.heading: The Petition
sections.body:
Membership in the United Federation of Planets begins with a request, never an invitation pressed on the unwilling. A world's government petitions the Federation Council, formally declaring its wish to join and its acceptance of the Federation Charter's obligations. The petition must come from an authority genuinely able to speak for the planet: the Federation admits worlds, not factions, and an application submitted by one nation or bloc among several is returned. This requirement alone has delayed candidacies for generations, since many otherwise qualified species reached the stars still politically divided.

Receipt of a petition opens a formal relationship. The Council assigns the candidacy to committee, diplomatic missions are exchanged, and the world's institutions are opened to Federation study — as the Federation's are opened in return. Nothing about the process is quick by design. Admission is treated as effectively permanent, so the examination is conducted on the assumption that both parties will live with the answer for centuries. Worlds have withdrawn petitions, resubmitted them decades later, and been welcomed; the door, Council practice holds, closes only from the inside.

sections.heading: Requirements for Admission
sections.body:
The formal requirements are few and strict. The candidate must possess a unified planetary government exercising effective authority. Its society must extend full rights to all its sentient inhabitants: caste discrimination is disqualifying, as is any legal order that sorts persons into ranks by birth. It must renounce aggressive war, accept the peaceful settlement of disputes, and demonstrate institutions stable enough to honour treaty obligations. Its record on fundamental rights is examined in depth, not merely its constitution's text.

By long convention the candidate is also expected to be a spacefaring culture, warp capability being the customary threshold — the same threshold that governs first contact, and for the same reason: a world that has reached the stars on its own has already met its neighbours. Records differ on whether warp flight is a requirement in law or an expectation in practice; the distinction has rarely been tested, since worlds below that threshold are shielded from contact by the Prime Directive itself. Wealth, size and military strength are pointedly absent from the criteria. Worlds of modest means sit as full members beside founding powers, with equal standing in the Council.

sections.heading: Candidacy and Evaluation
sections.body:
Between petition and admission lies the candidacy — commonly years long, sometimes decades. Federation study commissions examine the world's law, economy, sciences and civil institutions. Cultural exchange programmes begin; candidate officers may enter Starfleet Academy by sponsorship; trade agreements and mutual defence understandings are often concluded in the interim. The purpose is partly evaluation and partly rehearsal: by the time the Council votes, membership should formalise a relationship that already exists.

The examination reaches deeper than governments sometimes expect. In one instructive case, a divided world — where one hemisphere's state sought admission while its rival stood apart — pressed its application on the strength of its own qualifications. The Council declined to proceed; admitting half a planet would import the planet's quarrel into the Federation. Candidacies have also stalled over unresolved rights questions, over territorial disputes with neighbouring powers, and over the discovery that a government's writ was thinner than its diplomats claimed. A stalled candidacy is not a rejection: the file remains open, the objections are stated plainly, and the remedy is left with the candidate.

sections.heading: Admissions Debated and Deferred
sections.body:
Two cases dominate the historical record. The admission of Coridan was contested at the Babel Conference of 2267, one of the most fractious diplomatic assemblies of its century. Coridan's dilithium wealth had drawn competing claims and illegal mining interests among Federation members themselves; admission would extinguish those claims, and delegations arrived divided, with the Tellarite and Vulcan missions openly at odds and sabotage attempted en route. The conference ultimately favoured admission — and the affair remains the standing proof that Federation members bring interests as well as ideals to the chamber.

Bajor is the study in timing. Emerging from a brutal occupation, Bajor petitioned for membership and was formally accepted for admission in 2373 — whereupon its religious Emissary, Starfleet's own Captain Benjamin Sisko, counselled delay, and the Council of Ministers withdrew acceptance on the eve of signature. The decision looked inexplicable and proved providential: as a non-member, Bajor could sign a non-aggression pact that spared it the Dominion War's opening devastation. By most accounts membership followed in the years after the war, on a foundation the delay had strengthened.

sections.heading: What Membership Brings — and Costs
sections.body:
Admission is enacted by vote of the Federation Council and sealed by the candidate's signature of the Charter. From that hour the new member seats a Council delegation, enjoys the protection of Starfleet, and enters the largest zone of free exchange in known space — scientific, cultural and material. Its citizens gain Federation citizenship alongside their own, with every guarantee of Federation law. Its students enter Starfleet Academy by right rather than sponsorship.

The costs are equally real. The member cedes independent foreign and defence policy to the common institutions; its forces are integrated or stood down; its disputes with fellow members move to arbitration whose outcome it must accept. It accepts the Prime Directive's discipline toward worlds less advanced than itself, whatever its prior habits. And it binds its descendants: no mechanism of expulsion appears in the public record, and voluntary departure, while lawfully possible, is nearly unknown. Prospective members are told the sum plainly. The Federation is not a treaty of convenience but a shared civilisation, and a world that signs the Charter is not joining an alliance — it is joining a people.

guides.title: Starfleet Intelligence
guides.summary: Starfleet Intelligence is Starfleet's intelligence service, responsible for gathering and analysing information on foreign powers and threats to Federation security — and formally distinct from the rogue organisation known as Section 31.

sections.heading: Role Within Starfleet
sections.body:
Starfleet Intelligence is the branch of Starfleet charged with knowing what the Federation's rivals would prefer it did not. Its remit covers the collection, analysis and distribution of information bearing on Federation security: the disposition of foreign fleets, the intentions of hostile governments, the movements of hostile non-state actors, and the emergence of technologies that could shift the strategic balance. Its product reaches Starfleet Command, starship captains operating near contested borders, and, through the chain of command, the Federation President and Council.

The branch is a uniformed service, not a secret one. Its existence is acknowledged, its officers hold ordinary Starfleet ranks, and its conduct is bound by the same law and regulation as the rest of the fleet. That distinction matters in a quadrant where its counterparts — the Romulan Tal Shiar, the Cardassian Obsidian Order — operated as instruments of internal terror as much as foreign espionage. Starfleet Intelligence has no police power over Federation citizens, and its charter confines it to matters of external security.

sections.heading: Organisation and Methods
sections.body:
The bulk of intelligence work is unglamorous and analytical. Listening posts along the Neutral Zones intercept and decode signal traffic; long-range sensor networks track fleet movements; analysts cross-reference trade records, subspace chatter and diplomatic reporting to build assessments. Debriefing is a core discipline — defectors, released prisoners, and Starfleet crews returning from contested space are all interviewed, and a single well-placed defector has more than once rewritten the Federation's picture of an adversary.

Field operations exist but are the smaller part of the service. Officers have operated under cover on foreign soil, most often for reconnaissance or the verification of specific threats rather than sustained infiltration. Starfleet captains are also, in a limited sense, part of the apparatus: standing orders require vessels to report observations of military significance, making every ship on patrol a collection platform. Assessments are graded by confidence and circulated on a need-to-know basis, and the service is notoriously careful to distinguish what it knows from what it believes — a discipline learned from failures in which the two were confused.

sections.heading: Notable Operations and Failures
sections.body:
The service's record is mixed in the way of all intelligence services, with its failures better documented than its successes. It tracked the Romulan Star Empire through decades of official silence and correctly anticipated the Empire's re-emergence in the 2360s. During the Dominion crisis it identified the Founders' capacity for infiltration early, and its warnings drove the security reforms — blood screenings, phase-variance sweeps — adopted across Federation space. In the war that followed, its assessments of Dominion ship production and Cardassian politics shaped Allied strategy, including the groundwork for the events that brought the Romulan Star Empire into the war.

Its failures were instructive. The service did not foresee the Klingon invasion of Cardassia in 2372, and it repeatedly underestimated the Obsidian Order — most notably failing to detect the Order's construction of a secret fleet in the Orias system until a joint Tal Shiar operation ended in catastrophe. Changeling infiltrators reached senior positions on Earth despite every countermeasure. Analysts regard the era as the service's hardest schooling: an adversary that could wear any face defeated collection methods built for fleets and borders, and doctrine was rebuilt around verification rather than observation.

sections.heading: Starfleet Intelligence and Section 31
sections.body:
No account of Federation intelligence is complete without the organisation that claims to be its shadow. Section 31 is a self-appointed covert cabal that asserts descent from a provision of the original Starfleet Charter and answers, by its own account, to no one. It has conducted assassination, sabotage and biological warfare in the Federation's name — including the engineered disease deployed against the Founders during the Dominion War — methods categorically forbidden to Starfleet Intelligence.

The official position, stated repeatedly and at the highest levels, is that Section 31 is not part of Starfleet Intelligence, holds no lawful authority, and is regarded as a rogue element. The practical relationship is murkier: Section 31 has demonstrably recruited from Starfleet's ranks, drawn on its files, and operated with a freedom suggesting that, at minimum, parts of the command structure preferred not to look. Officers of Deep Space 9 forced the organisation partly into the light in the 2370s, and the cure to the Founder disease was ultimately handed over in defiance of it. The distinction between the two bodies is real, and the service insists on it; history will judge how clean the line was kept.

sections.heading: Oversight and Limits
sections.body:
Starfleet Intelligence operates under civilian authority. Its budget and mandate are set through the Federation Council, its senior appointments are answerable to Starfleet Command, and its officers remain subject to Starfleet's code of justice and to the courts. Surveillance of Federation citizens is outside its charter, and the service has no authority of arrest; where an investigation touches internal security, jurisdiction passes to civilian authorities or to Starfleet security proper.

These limits are periodically tested. The attempted military coup on Earth in 2372, organised by serving admirals under the banner of Changeling preparedness, demonstrated how security fear can curdle into overreach, and the era's debates over blood screenings rehearsed arguments that recur whenever the Federation is frightened. The service's defenders note that it stayed loyal in that crisis; its critics note that vigilance toward one's own institutions is precisely the lesson of it. The consensus position, taught at the Academy, is that intelligence exists to protect an open society and is only legitimate while the society remains open — a standard the Federation regards not as idealism but as the mission itself.

guides.title: Starfleet Medical
guides.summary: Starfleet Medical is the medical command of Starfleet, responsible for the health of crews across the fleet, the training of doctors and medical officers, xenobiology research, and quarantine authority throughout Federation space.

sections.heading: Mandate and Command Structure
sections.body:
Starfleet Medical is the branch of Starfleet charged with the physical and psychological wellbeing of every officer, crew member, and civilian under fleet care. Its remit runs from routine physicals aboard patrol vessels to planet-scale relief operations following famine, plague, or disaster, and it holds standing authority over medical policy on every commissioned starship and starbase.

The branch is headed by the Surgeon General of Starfleet, a flag officer who answers to Starfleet Command but exercises independent judgment on matters of medical ethics and public health. Beneath the Surgeon General sit the fleet medical divisions: shipboard services, starbase hospitals, emergency response, xenobiological research, and the long-term care facilities that treat officers invalided out of active service.

A distinctive feature of the command structure is that medical authority runs parallel to the ordinary chain of command rather than through it. A ship's chief medical officer reports to the captain for duty purposes, but on questions of fitness, contagion, and treatment the medical judgment is final. This dual structure was written into Starfleet's founding regulations and has survived every subsequent reorganization of the fleet.

sections.heading: Headquarters and Fleet Hospitals
sections.body:
Starfleet Medical maintains its headquarters in San Francisco on Earth, adjacent to the main Starfleet Command complex and Starfleet Academy. The headquarters campus combines a teaching hospital, research laboratories, and the administrative offices that set fleet-wide medical standards. Officers rotate through it between deep-space postings, and it is the customary destination for cases too complex or too dangerous for a shipboard sickbay.

Beyond Earth, the branch operates a network of starbase hospitals and dedicated medical facilities positioned along the major shipping and patrol lanes. These installations serve as trauma centers for the surrounding sectors, staging points for medical relief convoys, and quarantine stations for vessels returning from first-contact or biohazard situations.

In wartime the network expands rapidly. Hospital ships, purpose-built or converted from other classes, follow the fleet and take casualties directly from the line. Records of the Dominion War describe field hospitals processing thousands of wounded, with Starfleet Medical coordinating triage, evacuation, and the long convalescence that followed. The branch regards this surge capacity as a core obligation rather than an emergency improvisation.

sections.heading: Training Medical Officers
sections.body:
Physicians, nurses, and medical technicians enter the fleet through Starfleet Medical Academy, the branch's teaching institution. The course of study is deliberately broader than planetary medical training, because a shipboard doctor cannot refer a difficult case to a specialist across town. Graduates are expected to handle surgery, virology, toxicology, obstetrics, and psychiatry for their own species and to manage competent care for dozens of others.

Xenomedicine dominates the curriculum. A single starship crew may include humans, Vulcans, Andorians, Tellarites, Bolians, and Trill, each with distinct physiology, pharmacology, and disease profiles. Students learn comparative anatomy across Federation member species and, just as importantly, learn the diagnostic discipline needed when confronting a lifeform no database describes.

Clinical rotations take cadets through the San Francisco teaching hospital, starbase wards, and supervised postings aboard active vessels. The final examinations test judgment under failure conditions: sickbay without power, triage without a tricorder, treatment without consent when the patient is unconscious and the species unknown. Officers who pass receive both a medical degree and a commission, and most describe the two as inseparable.

sections.heading: Research and the Frontier of Medicine
sections.body:
Starfleet Medical operates one of the largest biomedical research establishments in the quadrant, driven by a simple pressure: exploration keeps finding diseases, injuries, and lifeforms that existing medicine cannot address. Every first contact adds physiology to the comparative databases, and every novel pathogen encountered by a starship is sequenced, catalogued, and distributed fleet-wide so that the next crew to meet it starts with an answer rather than a mystery.

Major research programs have included regenerative treatments for radiation and plasma injuries, synthetic blood and organ replacement, countermeasures for telepathic and neurological assault, and the containment of engineered plagues. The branch also maintains the fleet's protocols on Borg assimilation reversal, developed case by case as survivors were recovered.

Research is bounded by Federation medical ethics, and the boundaries are enforced. Experimentation on sentient beings without consent is prohibited regardless of the promised benefit, and records show researchers stripped of their licenses for violating that line. The branch's position is long established: medicine that abandons its ethics stops being medicine, however impressive its results.

sections.heading: Medical Authority Aboard Ship
sections.body:
The most visible expression of Starfleet Medical's independence is the standing of the chief medical officer aboard a starship. Under fleet regulations the CMO may examine any member of the crew, including the captain, and may certify an officer unfit for duty on medical or psychological grounds. In extreme cases the CMO can relieve a commanding officer of duty, a power granted to no other department head and hedged with strict procedural safeguards.

This authority exists because command decisions made by an impaired captain endanger the entire ship, and because no officer, however senior, can be trusted to diagnose their own incapacity. The regulation is invoked rarely and reviewed exhaustively afterward, but its existence shapes the relationship between captain and doctor on every bridge in the fleet.

Quarantine is the other pillar of shipboard medical power. A CMO may seal decks, restrict transporter use, and hold a vessel out of port when contagion is suspected, and Starfleet Medical's quarantine declarations bind civilian traffic as well as fleet vessels within Federation space. Captains have protested such orders; records do not show many succeeding.

guides.title: The Department of Temporal Investigations
guides.summary: The Department of Temporal Investigations is the Federation agency that investigates time travel incidents and temporal violations involving Starfleet officers and Federation citizens, and enforces the rules governing conduct in the past.

sections.heading: Mandate and Jurisdiction
sections.body:
The Department of Temporal Investigations is the Federation's standing authority on time travel. Its mandate is narrow and absolute: to investigate every credible temporal incident touching Federation citizens or Starfleet vessels, to determine whether history was altered, and to enforce the regulations that govern conduct in the past. Where a starship's log records a displacement — accidental slingshot effects, wormhole anomalies, encounters with temporally active artifacts or beings — the department's agents are dispatched as a matter of course, and command officers are obliged to submit to debriefing.

The department's authority is investigative rather than operational. It does not, so far as public record shows, conduct time travel itself; its business is the aftermath. Its agents hold clearance to review classified logs, impound temporally sensitive materials and require sworn testimony from officers of any rank. Within its own field it answers to the Federation Council, and its findings can end careers: a confirmed, avoidable alteration of the timeline is among the gravest charges a Starfleet officer can face.

sections.heading: How an Investigation Proceeds
sections.body:
A temporal investigation begins with the debrief. Agents interview every officer involved, separately and at length, reconciling testimony against sensor logs to reconstruct exactly what was changed, when, and by whom. The department's questions are famously exacting — whether an incident occurred three weeks ago or four matters greatly to investigators for whom the date of an event may be the least stable fact about it.

Findings are sorted into a taxonomy the department maintains with some rigour. Alterations are graded by scope and by reversibility. Predestination paradoxes — sequences in which the traveller's actions were always part of history and therefore changed nothing — occupy a special category; agents are known to dislike them professionally, since they close a file while resolving nothing. Where genuine alteration is found, the report assesses whether restoration was achieved, whether negligence was involved, and whether charges are warranted. Most investigations end quietly: the majority of recorded displacements are accidents, competently handled by crews who wanted nothing more than to get home. The department's files remain sealed at high classification, which its agents consider the natural condition of the subject.

sections.heading: Notable Cases on Record
sections.body:
The department's most cited file concerns Deep Space 9. In 2373 the crew of the USS Defiant was carried back to the year 2268 through the action of a Bajoran artifact, arriving at Deep Space Station K-7 in the middle of a documented crisis involving Klingon agents and a cargo of quadrotriticale. Agents Dulmur and Lucsly conducted the debrief of Captain Benjamin Sisko personally. The investigation concluded that history had been preserved — with the footnote that Sisko had spoken directly with Captain James Kirk, a liberty the department noted without endorsing.

Kirk himself occupies a unique position in the department's records: seventeen separate temporal violations are attributed to him, the largest file on any individual. Department folklore, in so far as so exacting an agency can be said to have folklore, holds him as the cautionary standard. Other significant files include the Enterprise-E's pursuit of a Borg sphere to the year 2063, where the launch of Zefram Cochrane's first warp flight had to be actively protected, and numerous smaller displacements that ended, after exhaustive interviews, with the timeline certified intact.

sections.heading: Doctrine, the Temporal Prime Directive, and the Accords
sections.body:
The department's doctrine descends from a simple principle: the past is not a resource. An officer displaced in time must avoid disclosure of future knowledge, minimise interaction, and restore the timeline where it has been damaged. In the late twenty-fourth century this hardened into the Temporal Prime Directive, which forbids interference with the timeline outright and places even discussion of certain future contacts under seal.

The department's relationship to the temporal powers of later centuries is documented only in fragments. Records establish that by the twenty-ninth century Starfleet itself operated timeships tasked with policing history, and that a body of agreements — the Temporal Accords — eventually bound signatory powers to renounce the offensive use of time travel. Records differ on how much of this the department of the current era knows officially, and its agents decline the question as a matter of policy. What is certain is that the department regards itself as the ancestor of that later order: the unglamorous, procedural insistence that history happened once, and ought to be left as found.

sections.heading: Working With the Department
sections.body:
Starfleet officers encounter the department at the worst possible moment: immediately after surviving something impossible. Standing orders are straightforward. Any temporal displacement, however brief, must be reported; logs must be preserved unedited; and crews must not compare recollections before interview, since honest disagreement between witnesses is itself evidence of alteration. Officers are advised to answer precisely, volunteer nothing, and resist the impulse to make the story tidy.

The agents themselves are a known quantity in the fleet. They travel in pairs, dress and speak with deliberate plainness, and are immune to charm by long practice — humour, in particular, is received as a delay. This manner is cultivated. The department's position is that time travel is the one field in which excitement is indistinguishable from damage, and its agents comport themselves accordingly. For all the fleet's jokes at their expense, commanders who have been through a temporal incident tend to speak of the department with respect: it is the only institution in the Federation whose entire purpose is to certify, after the impossible has happened, that the universe is still the one you left.

guides.title: The Federation Charter
guides.summary: The Federation Charter is the founding document of the United Federation of Planets, signed in 2161 by Earth, Vulcan, Andoria and Tellar, establishing the Council, the Presidency, Starfleet and the guarantees of individual rights.

sections.heading: Founding at the End of a War
sections.body:
The Charter of the United Federation of Planets was signed in 2161, in San Francisco on Earth, by the founding worlds: United Earth, the Confederacy of Vulcan, the Andorian Empire and the United Planets of Tellar. It was the direct product of a hard decade. The Earth-Romulan War had just ended, fought by an alliance of precisely those four powers, and the Coalition of Planets that preceded the war had shown both the value of common cause and the fragility of mere alliance. The Charter converted wartime partnership into permanent union.

The choice of Earth for the signing reflected Earth's peculiar position among the four: the youngest spacefaring power, and the one that had spent the previous decade as the alliance's connective tissue — trusted by Vulcan and Andoria in a way Vulcan and Andoria did not yet trust each other. Records of the ceremony describe delegations that had been at one another's throats within living memory signing a single document as equals. That image, more than any clause of the text, is what the Federation's later members say they joined.

sections.heading: What the Charter Establishes
sections.body:
The Charter constitutes the Federation's institutions and allocates their powers. It establishes the Federation Council as the supreme legislative body, seated on Earth, in which every member world holds representation; a Presidency, elected to head the executive and conduct foreign relations, with offices in Paris; and a judiciary culminating in the Federation Supreme Court. It commits the members to a common foreign policy, mutual defence, and the peaceful settlement of internal disputes, while reserving to each world the government of its own domestic affairs — the Federation was built as a union of distinct civilisations, not the dissolution of them.

The Charter also mandates a unified space service, and Starfleet was chartered alongside the Federation itself, absorbing the exploratory and defence services of the founding worlds. Notably, the founding documents fix Starfleet's primary mission as exploration and science, with defence as duty rather than purpose — a deliberate inversion of the wartime footing on which the founding powers had been operating, and one the Federation has reaffirmed after every subsequent war.

sections.heading: Guarantees and the Rights of the Individual
sections.body:
The Federation's founding law enumerates fundamental rights that no member government, and no organ of the Federation itself, may abridge. These Guarantees bind courts, commanders and councils alike. The Seventh Guarantee, protecting a person against self-incrimination, is the most cited in legal records; others secure due process, freedom of expression and conscience, and the equality of all sentient beings before the law — the principle under which caste discrimination disqualifies a world from membership. Later jurisprudence extended the Guarantees' protection to artificial and non-corporeal intelligences: holdings the founders did not foresee, but which their language, deliberately drafted in terms of sentient life rather than any species, proved able to carry.

Records differ on the precise architecture of the founding law. Sources refer variously to the Charter, to a Federation Constitution, and to the Fundamental Declarations of the Martian Colonies — an earlier rights instrument of the Earth sphere that the founders drew upon — and legal historians debate which guarantees originate in which text. The practice of the courts renders the debate academic: the Guarantees are enforced as a single continuous inheritance, and invoking one is sufficient to halt any proceeding in the Federation.

sections.heading: Contested Readings
sections.body:
One clause of the founding era has cast a long shadow. Operatives of the covert organisation calling itself Section 31 have claimed their authority from the original Starfleet Charter — citing, by their own account, an article whose thirty-first section acknowledged that extraordinary threats might justify extraordinary measures, and treating that acknowledgement as a standing licence for espionage, sabotage and assassination in the Federation's name. Mainstream jurists reject the reading root and branch: the provision, so far as its text can be established, created no agency, exempted no one from law, and cannot coherently authorise a body that answers to no institution the founding documents create.

The dispute is more than antiquarian. It illustrates the founding texts' one structural vulnerability — language written by pragmatists at the end of a war, generous enough to survive centuries, is generous enough to be abused. The Federation's answer has been institutional rather than textual: courts and councils have simply declined to recognise Section 31's claim whenever it has surfaced, and the organisation has operated as an outlaw of the very document it cites.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Charter has proved the most durable constitutional instrument in the quadrant's recorded history. From four worlds at its signing, the Federation grew past one hundred and fifty members within two centuries, and every admission since 2161 has been enacted the same way: by signature of the same document the founders signed. The text has been amended sparingly and reinterpreted continuously, in the manner of constitutions that succeed; its guarantees have been stretched over beings, technologies and situations the founders could not have imagined, and have mostly held.

Its endurance is not merely institutional. Records from far later eras — fragmentary, and touching matters still under temporal seal — indicate that a United Federation of Planets persisted into the thirty-second century, through crises that broke nearly every other power of the founders' age. Whether that continuity runs through the original Charter or its successors, the record does not clearly state. What the record does show is the pattern set in San Francisco in 2161 repeating at every scale since: former adversaries, given an honest text and equal standing, choosing to become one polity — the Federation's founding act, performed over and over.

guides.title: Starfleet's Judge Advocate General
guides.summary: The Judge Advocate General (JAG) is Starfleet's legal service, conducting courts-martial, boards of inquiry and legal hearings under Federation law, and the office behind landmark rulings such as the Data personhood hearing.

sections.heading: The Legal Arm of Starfleet
sections.body:
The office of the Judge Advocate General is Starfleet's judiciary and bar in one. Its officers — trained in Federation law and holding Starfleet commissions — prosecute and defend at courts-martial, preside over boards of inquiry, advise commanders on the legality of orders, and rule on questions of law that arise wherever the fleet operates. Every sector with a significant Starfleet presence maintains a JAG office; the officer heading such a command holds broad authority to convene hearings and issue rulings binding on Starfleet personnel within it.

The office's independence is deliberately protected. A JAG officer's rulings are not subject to command override; a starship captain who disagrees with a legal finding may appeal it, but may not countermand it. This arrangement reflects a principle the Federation inherited from the legal traditions of several founding worlds: that a service under arms remains lawful only if the people who judge it do not take orders from the people it judges. In practice the office is small, chronically overworked at frontier postings, and central to some of the most consequential decisions in Starfleet history.

sections.heading: Courts-Martial and Boards of Inquiry
sections.body:
A general court-martial is the fleet's gravest proceeding, reserved for capital charges and offences that could end a career. Convention requires a panel of command-grade officers to sit in judgment, with prosecution and defence counsel drawn from the JAG office or, at the accused's election, from any qualified advocate — officers have been defended by their own captains. Verdicts are reached on the record, and the accused enjoys the presumption of innocence, the right to confront evidence, and the right of appeal.

Below the court-martial sit lesser instruments. A board of inquiry establishes facts after a loss or incident without itself assigning criminal guilt; its findings determine whether charges follow. A competency hearing weighs an officer's fitness to serve or to stand trial. Extradition hearings decide whether personnel may be surrendered to foreign jurisdiction — proceedings that have carried heavy diplomatic freight when the requesting power's justice is summary. Through all of them runs the same machinery: sworn testimony, computer-verified records, and a JAG officer with the authority to compel both.

sections.heading: Landmark Hearings
sections.body:
Three proceedings are studied by every cadet. In 2267 Captain James Kirk stood general court-martial for the apparent death of Lieutenant Commander Benjamin Finney; the trial turned when his defence exposed the ship's computer record as falsified and the supposed victim as alive — an early and lasting lesson that machine testimony is evidence, not truth.

In 2365, at Starbase 173, Captain Phillipa Louvois of the sector JAG office ruled on whether Lieutenant Commander Data was Starfleet property or a person entitled to refuse an experimental procedure that might have destroyed him. Her ruling — that Data had the right to choose — stopped short of settling the metaphysics but established the precedent on which the legal standing of artificial beings in the Federation still rests.

In 2367 a routine inquiry aboard the Enterprise-D expanded into a spiralling hunt for conspiracy under Rear Admiral Norah Satie, until an invocation of the Seventh Guarantee and the words of her own jurist father collapsed the proceeding. The affair is taught as the office's cautionary tale: the forms of law can be turned against its substance, and a hearing can become a weapon.

sections.heading: Rights of the Accused
sections.body:
Federation military justice rests on guarantees older than Starfleet. The Federation's founding law enumerates protections for the individual; the Seventh Guarantee, shielding a person against self-incrimination, is the most frequently cited in fleet proceedings, and its invocation carries a weight that has stopped tribunals in their tracks. An accused officer is entitled to counsel of choice, to silence, to examination of all evidence, and to a verdict grounded in the record rather than in command convenience.

The guarantees extend further than some member worlds' own traditions. They have been held to protect officers of non-Federation origin serving in Starfleet, civilians under Starfleet jurisdiction, and — since the Data precedent — beings whose personhood was itself the question before the court. JAG doctrine treats the guarantees as floor, not ceiling: a proceeding may afford more protection than the minimum, never less. Officers are reminded that the guarantees bind most tightly precisely when they are least convenient, in wartime and in fear; the office's institutional memory holds that every historic failure of Federation justice began with an argument that this case was different.

sections.heading: The Office in Practice
sections.body:
Most JAG work never reaches a courtroom. Officers review rules of engagement before operations, advise captains on treaty obligations at contested borders, draft the legal annexes of first-contact protocols, and settle the small disputes — salvage claims, cargo liability, jurisdiction over crimes committed on leave — that a fleet of thousands of vessels generates continuously. On frontier stations a single JAG officer may serve as prosecutor, defender and judge in rotation, with safeguards to keep the roles from touching the same case.

Service in the office carries a particular reputation: it attracts officers who joined Starfleet for its principles rather than its adventures, and it is famously indifferent to rank. Admirals have been ruled against by lieutenants, and the rulings have held. The office's unofficial creed, passed between its officers rather than printed in any manual, is that Starfleet's weapons defend the Federation's existence, but its law defends the Federation's point — and of the two, the law is the harder posting.

guides.title: The Post-Scarcity Economy of the Federation
guides.summary: The Federation operates a post-scarcity economy: replicators and abundant energy have ended material want on its core worlds, money in the old sense has largely disappeared, and citizens work for purpose and reputation rather than wages.

sections.heading: What Post-Scarcity Means
sections.body:
By the twenty-fourth century the United Federation of Planets had ceased to be an economy of scarcity in any sense its founders would have recognized. Energy is abundant, matter can be synthesized on demand, and the material needs of a citizen — food, shelter, clothing, medicine, transport, education — are met as a matter of course rather than earned as a matter of survival. Poverty, in the old meaning of the word, does not exist on the Federation's developed worlds.

This is not a claim that everything is unlimited. Starships, dilithium, habitable land, orbital berths, and the time of skilled people remain finite, and the Federation allocates them through planning, priority, and negotiation rather than price. What ended was the condition in which ordinary life had to be purchased, and in which the failure to earn meant hunger.

Federation citizens describe the change less in economic terms than in moral ones. The elimination of want removed the oldest justification for acquisition, and the culture that grew up afterward treats the accumulation of possessions as an eccentricity rather than an achievement. Wealth, as one famous formulation has it, ceased to be the point.

sections.heading: The Replicator and the End of Material Want
sections.body:
The technological foundation of Federation abundance is the replicator, a matter-synthesis device derived from transporter technology that assembles food, tools, clothing, spare parts, and nearly any inanimate object from stored patterns and raw matter stock. A device that can produce a meal or a machine component on request, at negligible cost, collapses the supply chains around which older economies were organized.

Replication did not arrive all at once. Earlier generations relied on protein resequencers and synthesizers of more limited range, and the full food-and-goods replicator became standard on starships and in Federation homes only in the twenty-fourth century. Its spread tracked the availability of energy: a replicator is only as generous as the power grid behind it, and the Federation's investment in fusion and matter-antimatter generation is what made synthesis effectively free.

Limits remain. Certain materials, notably latinum, resist replication, and living beings cannot be replicated at all. Connoisseurs insist replicated food falls short of the grown and cooked original, and a quiet trade in real vegetables, vintage wines, and handmade goods persists — valued precisely because they were not synthesized. The Federation regards this as taste, not scarcity.

sections.heading: Work Without Wages
sections.body:
The commonest question outsiders ask of the Federation is why anyone works. The observable answer is that nearly everyone does. Starfleet officers accept years of danger and discipline; civilians farm, cook, teach, build, compose, and research; and the Federation's output of science, art, and engineering has grown, not shrunk, since compensation ceased to be the motive.

Federation citizens explain this without difficulty. When survival is guaranteed, work becomes the primary means by which a person improves themselves and their civilization; status attaches to competence, contribution, and reputation rather than to holdings. A celebrated chef who could replicate every dish chooses to cook; a family runs a vineyard the old way; an officer spends a career charting space no one is paying to have charted. The activity is the reward, and excellence is the currency.

Critics from market cultures, the Ferengi foremost among them, have called the arrangement naive and predicted its collapse for over a century. The prediction has not aged well. The Federation's difficulty is not motivating its citizens but choosing among the volunteers, and its institutions ration opportunity — a posting, a commission, a laboratory — far more often than they ration goods.

sections.heading: Money at the Edges
sections.body:
The disappearance of money inside the Federation did not abolish it at the borders. The interstellar economy beyond Federation space runs on currency, most famously gold-pressed latinum, a liquid metal that cannot be replicated and therefore holds value in an age of synthesis. Ferengi commerce, independent traders, frontier stations, and a good deal of quiet diplomacy are conducted in latinum, and Federation citizens who live or work along the frontier handle it as a practical necessity.

Starfleet crews stationed at posts such as Deep Space 9 learned this fluency quickly: bar tabs, holosuite time, and dabo tables operate on Ferengi rules, and an officer's principled explanation that their civilization has evolved beyond money settles no account. The Federation itself maintains instruments for external trade and reimbursement, and references to Federation credits appear throughout the records of both the twenty-third and twenty-fourth centuries.

How those credits functioned internally is genuinely unclear, and records differ. Some accounts treat them as an accounting convenience for allocation and offworld exchange; others suggest earlier eras retained more conventional transactions than later citizens liked to recall. The honest summary is that the Federation's abandonment of money was real, gradual, and never total at its edges.

sections.heading: Allocation, Land, and the Things That Stay Scarce
sections.body:
A post-scarcity society still makes choices. Starship hulls, dilithium crystals, terraforming equipment, and antimatter stocks are produced and allocated deliberately, through Federation and Starfleet planning rather than markets. A colony's request for an industrial replicator is weighed against every other colony's; the loss of even a few such units is significant enough to appear in diplomatic records. Scarcity was not abolished so much as moved up the scale, from the dinner table to the shipyard.

Position and place remain finite as well. There is one captaincy per starship, one plot of coastline per house, one seat in a celebrated orchestra. The Federation allocates these by merit, seniority, and choice, and its citizens compete for them with an intensity that surprises visitors expecting a society without ambition.

The system's admirers call it the first economy organized around human flourishing rather than exchange; its critics note that planning has quiet politics of its own. Both observations are true. What is not in dispute is the outcome on the ground: in the Federation's core, no child is hungry, no illness goes untreated for cost, and no one's life is spent earning the right to continue it.

guides.title: The Vulcan Science Academy
guides.summary: The Vulcan Science Academy is Vulcan's foremost institution of research and higher learning, an academy renowned across the Federation for the rigor of its admissions, the depth of its science, and the logic that governs its scholars.

sections.heading: Standing on Vulcan and Beyond
sections.body:
The Vulcan Science Academy, located in the city of Shi'Kahr on Vulcan, is widely regarded as the preeminent scientific institution of its world and among the most respected in the entire Federation. For a Vulcan, admission is not merely an educational opportunity but a mark of intellectual distinction recognized across their society; families measure standing in part by the generations they have sent through its halls.

The Academy predates Vulcan's membership in the Federation by a considerable margin. Vulcan science was already ancient when humans first achieved warp flight, and the Academy carries that inheritance: its archives hold observational records, mathematical proofs, and philosophical treatises accumulated over centuries of disciplined inquiry.

Within the Federation scientific community the Academy occupies a position comparable to Starfleet's own research commands and the great universities of Earth, though it remains a distinctly Vulcan institution rather than a Federation one. Its findings circulate freely among member worlds, but its governance, admissions, and methods answer to Vulcan tradition. Offworld scholars describe collaboration with the Academy as invaluable and exacting in equal measure.

sections.heading: Admission and the Standard of Excellence
sections.body:
Admission to the Vulcan Science Academy is famously difficult, even by the standards of a species that treats intellectual discipline as a birthright. Candidates are evaluated across the full range of the sciences as well as logic, ethics, and the capacity for sustained independent research. The Academy does not grade on potential; it admits those who have already demonstrated mastery and rejects the rest without sentiment.

The admissions council interviews candidates directly, and its questions are remembered by generations of applicants as instruments of precision. The council probes not only what a candidate knows but how the candidate thinks: whether conclusions follow from evidence, whether uncertainty is acknowledged honestly, whether the applicant can be provoked into asserting more than the data supports.

Refusal of an offered place is nearly unheard of, which is why the case of Spock, son of Sarek, remains notable in the Academy's records. Offered admission, he chose instead to enter Starfleet Academy on Earth, a decision that strained his family and became famous well beyond Vulcan. The Academy's records treat the episode with characteristic economy: an offer was extended; it was declined.

sections.heading: Disciplines and Research Programs
sections.body:
The Academy's research spans the physical sciences, with particular eminence in subspace physics, astrophysics, planetary science, and mathematics. Vulcan contributions to warp theory, sensor design, and stellar cartography have shaped Federation technology for two centuries, and much of that work originated in or passed through the Academy's laboratories.

The life sciences hold an equally established place. Vulcan medicine, neurology, and the formal study of telepathic phenomena are pursued at the Academy with a depth few institutions can match, since the Vulcan mind itself, with its disciplines of meld and memory, presents research questions no offworld university can study from the inside. The Academy's work on the katra, the living essence Vulcans hold to persist beyond death, sits at the boundary of science and tradition, and its scholars are careful to mark where evidence ends and doctrine begins.

Applied programs exist but are subordinate to fundamental research. The Academy builds instruments, not products; its position is that understanding precedes application, and that a civilization which reverses that order eventually mistakes its tools for its knowledge.

sections.heading: Governance and the Discipline of Logic
sections.body:
The Academy is governed by a council of senior scholars, with ministers and administrators drawn from its own ranks. Decisions are reached through structured argument in which rank carries no evidentiary weight: a junior researcher whose data are sound expects to prevail over a council elder whose data are not, and the institution regards this as ordinary procedure rather than boldness.

Logic governs method as well as governance. Hypotheses are stated so that they can fail; results are published with their uncertainties attached; and error, once demonstrated, is corrected without ceremony. The Academy's culture treats attachment to a disproven idea as an emotional indulgence, which on Vulcan is a serious charge.

History records that this confidence has occasionally hardened into conservatism. Vulcan's scientific establishment in earlier eras held firmly to positions later shown incomplete, including long-standing skepticism about phenomena at the edges of accepted physics, and records differ on how gracefully individual councils absorbed correction. The Academy's own historians acknowledge the pattern and cite it in training as a caution: logic applied to incomplete premises yields rigorous error.

sections.heading: The Academy and Starfleet
sections.body:
Relations between the Vulcan Science Academy and Starfleet are close, continuous, and quietly competitive. The two institutions exchange researchers, share sensor data from across the quadrant, and jointly staff scientific expeditions where Starfleet supplies the ships and the Academy supplies a depth of theoretical grounding the fleet openly admires. Many Vulcan officers in Starfleet's science divisions trained first at the Academy or studied under its graduates.

The competition lies in philosophy. The Academy pursues knowledge as an end; Starfleet pursues it in the course of exploration, diplomacy, and defense, and accepts the compromises that mixed mandate requires. Academy scholars have been known to observe that a laboratory aboard a starship is a laboratory that may be asked to fire phasers, and Starfleet scientists have replied that a laboratory that never leaves orbit studies only what arrives.

Both institutions consider the argument productive. Candidates on Vulcan weigh the two paths as genuinely different lives: the Academy offers depth, continuity, and the company of the finest minds of a contemplative civilization; Starfleet offers the unknown itself. That the choice is real, and occasionally famous, is testimony to the standing of both.

guides.title: The United Federation of Planets
guides.summary: The interstellar union at the centre of the setting: what it is, how it governs, and why it holds together.

sections.heading: What the Federation Is
sections.body: The United Federation of Planets is a voluntary union of worlds rather than an empire. Member states retain their own governments, laws and cultures, and delegate to the Federation only those matters that cannot sensibly be handled world by world: interstellar defence, exploration, diplomacy with powers outside the union, and the maintenance of a common body of law. A world joins by application and by consent, and in principle it may leave the same way. That distinction is the whole political argument of the setting. The Federation's rivals are almost all empires that grew by conquest, and their standing objection is that a union assembled by agreement must be weaker than one assembled by force. The Federation's answer is that it is not, and most of its history is an argument about whether that answer holds. Its founding is conventionally dated to the mid-twenty-second century, when four powers that had recently been at odds with one another — humans, Vulcans, Andorians and Tellarites — signed a charter binding them into a single polity. The choice of those four is deliberate in the telling: they are temperamentally incompatible. Vulcans distrust human impulsiveness, Andorians and Vulcans had a long history of confrontation, and Tellarites regard argument itself as a form of courtesy. The union works not because its members are alike but because they agreed on a procedure for disagreeing. By the twenty-fourth century the Federation spans a substantial volume of the galaxy and counts its membership in the scores of worlds, with a much larger number of colonies, protectorates and associated states. Its capital is on Earth, in San Francisco, which is a source of quiet friction: a union of equals whose administrative centre sits on one member's homeworld invites the charge that it is a human project wearing a wider name.

sections.heading: How It Governs
sections.body: Authority rests with a Federation Council, seated in San Francisco, to which member worlds send representatives. The Council legislates, ratifies treaties, admits new members and holds the power of the purse. Its presiding officer is the Federation President, elected rather than inherited, who directs foreign policy and serves as civilian commander-in-chief of Starfleet. The presidency is deliberately drawn as an office of persuasion more than command; a president who cannot carry the Council carries very little. Federation law sits above member law in the areas the charter reserves, and below it everywhere else. The charter guarantees a set of individual rights that no member may abridge — protection from self-incrimination, from arbitrary detention, and from discrimination on the basis of species or origin among them. Admission requires a candidate world to meet those guarantees, to have a unified planetary government, and to have achieved faster-than-light travel on its own. That last condition is not a technical hurdle so much as a moral one: it is the point at which a civilisation has plainly discovered the wider galaxy for itself rather than having it revealed to them. Economically the Federation is usually described as post-scarcity, which is more a statement about energy and replication than about desire. When matter can be assembled from stored energy on demand, the classic problems of distribution largely dissolve, and with them much of the machinery of currency within Federation space. What does not dissolve is scarcity of the things that cannot be replicated: land on a pleasant world, the attention of a gifted teacher, an original work, a position on a ship going somewhere interesting. Federation society is organised around competition for those instead.

sections.heading: Membership and Its Frictions
sections.body: The union is not placid. Its recurring internal argument is between worlds that regard the Federation as primarily an exploratory and scientific enterprise and those that regard it as primarily a mutual-defence pact, and the balance between those readings shifts with how dangerous the neighbourhood happens to be. Long peace favours the explorers; a war on the border favours the admirals, and the setting repeatedly examines what the union becomes when the admirals are winning that argument. A second friction is the pace of expansion. Each admission adds strength and adds obligation: a new member's borders become everyone's borders to defend, and its quarrels become everyone's diplomacy. Worlds on the frontier periodically complain that the core makes policy for them without living with the consequences, which is the ordinary complaint of any federation that has grown faster than its sense of itself. A third is the status of colonies and non-member worlds inside Federation space. A colony is not a member; its people are Federation citizens but their settlement has no Council seat, and when a treaty redraws a border a colony can find itself traded away by a government it helped elect. That situation recurs often enough in the setting to function as a standing critique: a union founded on consent still contains people whose consent is not separately asked.

sections.heading: Why It Matters to the Setting
sections.body: The Federation exists in these stories to be a thesis under test. Nearly every antagonist it meets embodies an argument against it. An empire built on conquest argues that strength is the only real currency. A collective that assimilates argues that individuality is inefficiency. A civilisation built on genetic caste argues that equality is sentimentality. A rival that trades in profit argues that idealism is a luxury financed by replicators. The Federation is not written as automatically right in these encounters; it is written as obliged to answer. Its most interesting failures are therefore self-inflicted. Where the Federation is shown at its worst it is not overwhelmed from outside but tempted from within: by intelligence services that decide the charter is a peacetime document, by admirals who conclude the Council is too slow, by the argument that a sufficiently large threat licenses a small betrayal of principle. The recurring verdict is that a union which abandons its procedure to survive has not survived as itself. For a reader coming to this database, the practical point is that "the Federation" is rarely the answer to a question of fact. It is the frame in which the question is being asked: an institution whose stated values are unusually explicit, and which is repeatedly placed in situations designed to find out whether it means them.

guides.title: Starfleet
guides.summary: The Federation's combined exploratory, scientific, diplomatic and defensive service — and its deliberate refusal to be simply a navy.

sections.heading: A Service With Four Jobs
sections.body: Starfleet is the Federation's uniformed service, and the persistent question about it — asked inside the setting as often as outside — is what kind of service it actually is. Its charter gives it four tasks at once: to explore, to conduct science, to represent the Federation diplomatically, and to defend it. Those tasks are not obviously compatible. A ship optimised for a five-year survey of unmapped space is not the ship you would design to hold a border, and an officer trained to open relations with an unfamiliar civilisation is not obviously the officer you want commanding a battle line. Starfleet's answer is to insist that the same vessel and the same officer do all four, and to treat the tension as a feature. A ship that arrives as an explorer rather than a warship changes what the encounter can become; a captain who has been trained to negotiate will look for the negotiated outcome before the tactical one. The service is emphatic that it is not a military organisation, and equally emphatic that it maintains military discipline, rank and armament — a position its rivals find either hypocritical or incomprehensible, and which the stories examine rather than resolve. In practice the balance shifts. In quiet decades Starfleet reads as a scientific and exploratory corps with defensive capability. Under sustained threat it reorganises visibly towards war, and the setting treats that drift as a loss even when it is necessary — the argument being that a service which forgets it was meant to explore will eventually stop finding anything worth defending.

sections.heading: Structure, Rank and Command
sections.body: Starfleet is organised into commands and divisions under Starfleet Command, headquartered on Earth, which answers to the civilian Federation government. That subordination is treated as load-bearing: several of the setting's darkest turns involve senior officers deciding that civilian oversight is an obstacle rather than the point. Its rank structure follows naval convention — ensign, lieutenant, commander, captain, and the flag ranks above them — and its shipboard organisation divides personnel by function. In the earliest era those functions were signalled by uniform colour: command and helm in one shade, sciences and medicine in another, engineering, security and operations in a third. Later eras reassign the colours but keep the principle, which is that a crewman's role should be legible across a crowded compartment at a glance. Command of a starship is drawn as an unusually lonely job. A captain operating at the range these ships operate at is frequently beyond consultation, and is expected to make decisions that are properly political — whether to intervene, whom to recognise, what to promise — with no instruction and no appeal. The service's answer to that exposure is a heavy investment in the judgement of individuals rather than in the specificity of rules, which is why so much of the setting turns on what a particular officer decides to do when the regulation does not quite fit.

sections.heading: The Academy and the Officer It Wants
sections.body: Starfleet Academy, in San Francisco, is the service's principal officer school, and admission is competitive to a degree that becomes a plot point in its own right. The curriculum is deliberately broad — command theory, engineering, xenobiology, exobotany, diplomacy, tactics, law — on the reasoning that an officer at extreme range will need to be adequate at everything rather than excellent at one thing. The Academy is best known for a training scenario designed to be unwinnable. Its purpose is not to test tactics but to observe how a candidate behaves in the presence of certain defeat, on the argument that a commander will one day face a situation with no good outcome and the service needs to know in advance what they do there. The scenario's fame inside the setting rests on a cadet who declined to accept its premises and altered the test, and on the fact that the service commended rather than expelled him — an ambiguity the stories return to often. What Starfleet says it wants is curiosity restrained by discipline. What it repeatedly rewards is officers who disobey correctly. That gap is not a writing inconsistency so much as the service's central problem: a fleet operating beyond recall cannot function without initiative, and cannot function on initiative alone.

sections.heading: Starfleet in Practice
sections.body: Day to day, a Starfleet vessel does unglamorous work: charting, surveying, ferrying, mediating colonial disputes, delivering medical supplies, escorting convoys, maintaining relay networks. The exceptional encounters that dominate the record are exceptional precisely because the baseline is routine. The service's standing orders reflect that ordinariness. General Order One, the non-interference directive, governs contact with civilisations that have not developed interstellar flight. Other standing orders cover quarantine, the surrender of a vessel, the obligation to render aid, and the conditions under which a commanding officer may be relieved — that last one being the mechanism by which the setting examines what happens when a captain is genuinely unfit and the chain of command has to act against itself. Starfleet also maintains a small number of institutions that sit uneasily inside a service that calls itself non-military: an intelligence arm, a judge advocate general's corps, and — in the setting's less comfortable material — an unacknowledged organisation that claims to act for the Federation's survival outside any oversight at all. The existence of that last body is treated as a genuine indictment, and the argument against it is the same argument the Federation makes against its enemies: an institution that exempts itself from its own rules has already lost the thing it says it is protecting.

guides.title: The Prime Directive
guides.summary: General Order One: what non-interference actually requires, why it is drawn so absolutely, and the cases that test it.

sections.heading: The Rule Itself
sections.body: General Order One, universally called the Prime Directive, forbids Starfleet personnel from interfering in the natural development of a civilisation that has not achieved faster-than-light travel. In its strongest formulation it prohibits not merely conquest or coercion but contact of any kind: no revealing the existence of interstellar civilisation, no supplying technology, no taking sides in a local conflict, no correcting a local injustice, and — at its most demanding — no intervention even to prevent a natural catastrophe that will destroy the civilisation entirely. The rule binds harder the more senior the officer. It is drawn as the one order a captain may not set aside on their own judgement, which is deliberate: every other standing order in the service assumes that a commander at range must be trusted to adapt, and this one assumes the opposite. The service's position is that the temptation to help is precisely what makes the prohibition necessary, because the officer who intervenes is always convinced they are the exception. The reasoning offered is historical rather than abstract. Contact between a civilisation and a far more capable one has a poor record. The less capable society does not simply acquire the newcomer's technology; it acquires the newcomer's assumptions, loses confidence in its own institutions, and reorganises itself around a power it cannot match. The damage is done by arriving, not by intending harm.

sections.heading: Why It Is Drawn So Absolutely
sections.body: A rule with exceptions is a rule that will be argued away in the field, and the Prime Directive is written by people who expect it to be argued away. Nearly every case that reaches an officer will look like the exception: a plague that could be cured, a famine that could be fed, a war that could be stopped, a world that will be sterilised by its own star. The directive's answer is that an officer standing in front of a suffering they can end is the least reliable judge available of whether ending it is wise. There is a second argument, less often stated and more uncomfortable: that non-interference protects the interferer. A Federation that decides which civilisations deserve rescue has appointed itself an arbiter of who lives, and there is no version of that role that does not end in empire — however benevolent the first decision was. The directive is as much a constraint on the Federation's self-conception as a protection for anyone else. The strongest objection inside the setting is the obvious one. A rule that permits a civilisation to be extinguished by an asteroid, when a ship in orbit could deflect it in an afternoon, has elevated a principle above every life it applies to. The stories do not settle this. They tend instead to place officers in exactly that position and let the audience watch what the decision costs, whichever way it goes.

sections.heading: How It Fails in the Field
sections.body: The directive's practical failures fall into recognisable patterns. The first is contamination by accident: a ship observed, a crewman stranded, equipment left behind. A civilisation that finds a piece of technology it cannot make will build a religion or a war around it, and the setting returns repeatedly to societies deformed by a fragment of contact nobody meant to make. The second is the pre-existing contamination. An officer arrives to find a world already distorted by an earlier visit — sometimes by another power, sometimes by the Federation's own past — and must decide whether the directive forbids intervention or now requires it, since the natural development it protects has already been derailed. This is the case that most often produces a defensible violation. The third is the disguised intervention: acting through a proxy, arranging an outcome without appearing, deciding that concealment satisfies the rule. The setting is consistently sceptical of this reading. Non-interference is not a rule about being seen. The fourth, and the one treated most harshly, is the officer who invokes the directive to avoid a hard decision rather than to honour a principle. A rule that forbids acting is enormously convenient for anyone who did not want to act, and Starfleet's institutional contempt for that use of it is one of the clearer moral positions the setting takes.

sections.heading: What It Says About the Federation
sections.body: The Prime Directive is the Federation's most conspicuous attempt to bind itself in advance. A power that can do almost anything to a less capable neighbour has to decide, before it is tempted, what it will not do — and it has to decide it as a rule rather than as an intention, because intentions do not survive contact with an emergency. Read that way the directive is less about the protected civilisation than about the protector. It is the mechanism by which a union of enormous capability declines to become an empire of enormous capability, and it works by removing the decision from the person best placed to rationalise it. This is why violations are treated so gravely even when the outcome was good. An officer who saves a world in defiance of the order has, in the service's view, done two things: rescued a civilisation, and established that the rule bends for a sufficiently sympathetic case. The second is regarded as the more consequential, because every subsequent officer will now be weighing their own case against that precedent. The directive is, in short, the setting's clearest statement that the difficulty of a principle is not evidence against it — and its most honest admission that holding to one has a body count.

guides.title: Starfleet Academy
guides.summary: Where officers are made: admission, the four years, and the tests that are not about the subject.

sections.heading: Admission
sections.body: Entry to Starfleet Academy is competitive to a degree that shapes the character of everyone who gets in. Candidates sit a lengthy battery of examinations covering the sciences, mathematics, engineering and languages, alongside psychological assessment and physical qualification. Sponsorship by a serving officer is customary. Failure is common, reapplication is normal, and the setting takes some care to show respected officers who were rejected the first time. The competitive element is not only academic. Because the Federation is a coalition of many worlds, the entrance process must evaluate candidates whose education, physiology and cultural assumptions differ enormously, and must do so without simply advantaging whoever most resembles the assessors. That problem is never entirely solved, and cadets from smaller or more distant member worlds have a recognisable set of complaints about it. Non-member species may attend, usually as exchange cadets under an arrangement negotiated between governments. Such cadets occupy an awkward position — held to Starfleet standards while representing somewhere else — and the setting uses them to look at the institution from outside.

sections.heading: Four Years, and What They Are For
sections.body: The programme runs four years for most officer candidates, combining a broad core in sciences, history, ethics and command theory with specialisation in a chosen branch. Cadets serve practical assignments, including time aboard training vessels, and the fourth year in particular is heavily weighted toward operating under real conditions rather than in classrooms. The curriculum is deliberately broader than a strictly military academy would require. An officer may be the only qualified person present when a first contact occurs, when a medical emergency arrives, or when a legal question has to be answered light-years from anyone competent to answer it. Starfleet's answer to that is to teach everyone a great deal more than their job strictly needs. Discipline is real but unusual in emphasis. The Academy punishes dishonesty far more severely than incompetence, on the reasoning that an officer who conceals a mistake is more dangerous than one who makes it. Expulsions in the setting are almost always for lying, and almost never for failure.

sections.heading: The Tests That Are Not About the Subject
sections.body: The Academy's most discussed assessment is a command simulation constructed so that it cannot be won. A cadet is presented with a distress call inside hostile territory; answering it means violating a treaty and losing the ship, and ignoring it means abandoning civilians. Every possible action ends badly, and the cadet is graded on how they conduct themselves while it does. The stated purpose is to examine a candidate's relationship with failure before they are in a position to inflict it on a real crew. Officers who have taken it describe it as the moment they understood that command is not a set of problems with answers. The setting's most famous response to it — reprogramming the simulation on the grounds that no-win situations should not be accepted as given — is treated as both cheating and a legitimate display of the quality being tested, which is the point. Other assessments follow the same shape: survival exercises where the exercise is cooperation, ethics seminars where the seminar is whether you will say the unpopular thing. The Academy is consistently more interested in character than in knowledge, having concluded that knowledge is the easier of the two to supply.

sections.heading: Afterwards
sections.body: Graduates commission as ensigns and are posted, usually to a starship, occasionally to a starbase or a planetary facility. The first posting is understood by everyone involved to be a continuation of training by other means, and a good first captain is regarded as the single largest factor in how an officer's career goes. Advanced training exists for specialists — medical officers, engineers and scientists typically add postgraduate study, and command school is a separate qualification undertaken later. Enlisted personnel follow an entirely different route through technical schools and service, and the setting is inconsistent about how permeable the boundary between the two tracks is. The Academy also functions as the institution's memory. Its instructors are frequently officers rotated back from the field, its curriculum is revised after every significant failure, and its graduates carry a shared frame of reference that lets strangers from opposite ends of Federation space work together within an hour of meeting. That is a substantial part of what makes the fleet function at all.

guides.title: Starfleet Rank and the Chain of Command
guides.summary: Who outranks whom, what a rank actually authorises, and why the chain matters most when it is inconvenient.

sections.heading: The Ladder
sections.body: Starfleet commissioned ranks run, in ascending order, ensign, lieutenant junior grade, lieutenant, lieutenant commander, commander and captain, above which sit the flag ranks — commodore or rear admiral, vice admiral, admiral and fleet admiral, with the exact set varying by era. Below the commissioned ranks are the enlisted and non-commissioned grades, headed by the chief petty officer, whose practical authority within their specialty routinely exceeds their nominal position. Rank and post are separate things, and confusing them causes most of the misunderstandings outsiders have about the fleet. A commander may hold the post of first officer aboard a large vessel or command a small one outright. A captain by rank is not necessarily the captain of anything. Aboard ship, the officer in the command chair holds the authority of the post regardless of who else is present. The honorific complicates matters further: whoever commands a vessel is addressed as captain aboard it, whatever their rank. This is courtesy rather than promotion, and the setting uses the gap between the two for a good deal of quiet drama.

sections.heading: What a Rank Authorises
sections.body: Progression through the ranks is a progression in discretion rather than in expertise. An ensign executes. A lieutenant runs a watch or a section and answers for it. A lieutenant commander typically heads a department, owning both its readiness and its people. A commander as first officer runs the ship day to day so that the captain does not have to, and is expected to be the person who says the unwelcome thing in private. The captain's authority is the setting's central object of interest because it is so unusually broad. A starship captain may negotiate treaties, exercise judicial powers, conduct first contact, and commit the Federation to positions it has not agreed to — all because the alternative, waiting weeks for instructions, is worse. Flag officers direct fleets and set policy, and the setting is candid that distance from the deck is itself a hazard to judgement. Every level carries a duty to refuse an unlawful order, and Starfleet writes this down rather than leaving it implied. An officer who obeys an order they knew to be unlawful is liable for having obeyed it.

sections.heading: Succession and the Line
sections.body: Command devolves in a defined order — captain, first officer, second officer, then by seniority — and the line is published so that nobody has to work it out during a crisis. Departmental heads who are not in the command line still have absolute authority within their specialty, which produces the fleet's two well-known inversions. The first is medical. A chief medical officer may relieve any officer, including the captain, on grounds of fitness for duty.
